Initial thoughts:
Goddamn! The energy coursing through me as I watched this was insane. I sat up and damn near cheered from some of those needle drops. When '99 Luftballons' started playing during that crazy ass drug deal scene, holy shiiiiiiiit. THAT TIME I CHEERED I CAN'T LIE. I MAYBE CLAPPED A BIT TOO.

Characters/Acting
This PTA fella seriously knows how to create a web of characters that all feel interconnected while staying distinct and independently interesting. So many moments were teed up earlier in the film, both between characters, and in the character's own storylines. Most notably, the parallels between Eddie/Dirk and Rollergirl, both of them losing their battles at the same time.

William H. Macy's character just existing, and the running gag of his wife cheating, is on it's own one of the best thing's about this film. Alfred Molina during the drug deal scene is just so incredibly fun to watch. "Oh, that's Cosmo, he's Chinese" HAHAH, best delivered line of the entire film right there. Philip Seymour Hoffman as Scotty is the funniest shit ever, one of the best from him, and in my opinion the best in this film, however small a role. Julianne Moore as Amber is heartbreaking in the best way possible. 

Editing:
And it's that moment that exemplifies part of what makes the energy of this film so palpable: the editing. The ball is not dropped for a single moment here; just like in Magnolia, the way scenes are spliced together with such finesse is thoroughly felt. What's more is that while these cuts are in quick succession, they never lack intention nor do they ever feel jarring. 

The editor of both 'Magnolia' and 'Boogie Nights', Dylan Tichenor, in both films managed to maintain, and more importantly, amplify what shines most about each film. In Magnolia, the sprawling storyline of the entire ensemble and the through-line of grappling with complicated parent-child relationships is what shines most.

In Boogie Nights it's how slick and flashy everything feels while on the inside its actually crumbling. It's the 'maintaining appearances' of filmmaking. It's so smooth and exciting, and the soundtrack compliments the style so perfectly. But we cut away before learning more about Amber's divorce beyond that brief scene with her ex-husband; we never learn about how Eddie actually feels after being beaten up, we never learn how Rollergirl actually feels about her circumstances. And at the end of all this? a pseudo-happy ending where everything is framed as being 'just how it was'. I forfeit that it's the script and writing that made those decisions rather than the editing, but the impact of those decisions, in my opinion, is felt through the editing.

I love how the movie had two very different halves to it. It takes away the danceable energy shown in the first half and instead has a minimal use of a soundtrack. (Review initially written as part of a feminist analysis class- my opinion of the films craft is that it is extremely good, if the worst of the three PTAs I've seen)

Something frequently brought up in discussions of Boogie Nights, both negatively and positively, is that Paul Thomas Anderson was only 26 when he made it. Frankly, it’s no big stretch of the imagination that a white male twentysomething would come up with a rather blatant Goodfellas riff about the porn industry, starring Mark Wahlberg as Eddie Adams/Dirk Diggler, a young man who literally gets famous off of how big his dick is, but I think one of Boogie Nights’s most interesting and laudable qualities is how it wrestles with that juvenility, particularly the kind of frat-boy nonsense that such a concept would become in a lesser writer’s hands. That’s not to say that it wins, exactly- the one time this film passes the Bechdel Test is a girl asking a woman to be her mother while they’re both coked up to the gills, and the infamous (and beautiful) New Year’s Eve murder-suicide happens because William H. Macy’s bitch wife won’t stop undermining his masculinity by literally fucking other men in front of him. However, the other repeated talking point about Boogie Nights is its incredible sense of warmth and empathy, and one of the many, many effects of that kind narrative eye is that the women in this film are almost never leered at by the camera, the male gaze being conceptually sidestepped not through a lack of TnA, but through those tits and asses belonging to someone the script and camera love and care about. 

We see a lot of Julianne Moore’s cleavage and fully see Heather Graham’s vagina, but Graham’s Rollergirl/Brandy gets her own subplots about the harassment her occupation brings her, and her attempts to “go straight” by getting a GED, and Moore’s Amber Waves/Maggie is a deeply layered, tragic character, a woman lost in a toxic, depraved parody of motherhood as coke and society endlessly ruin her attempts to be a real mother. That in and of itself is kind of a patriarchal narrative, one that has her exist for men (the child she can’t see is a son, notably), but it’s also a fundamentally compassionate and humanizing one, born out of Director/Writer Paul Thomas Anderson’s legitimate affection for the people who work in the porn industry, on the basis of them being social outcasts trying to make something out of “filth”. This empathy is both the film’s greatest political strength and greatest political weakness- it pushes PTA to treat Philip Seymour Hoffman’s ugly, stuttering homosexual Scotty J as a lovable, if pitiable human being where almost any other white male 20something of his generation would make him a sideshow freak, but it also pushes him to treat Burt Reynolds’s Jack Horner, the man who recruited the (unknowingly to him) possibly mentally disabled and (knowingly to him) underage Eddie Adams into pornography, with kid gloves.

Cards on the table- I am a white male 20something who frequently consumes pornography both real and drawn, so I don’t consider the practice inherently evil by any stretch. However, Boogie Nights itself makes much hay of the exploitative and abusive nature of the 70s porn industry, with the entire character of The Colonel existing to demonstrate that exploitation at it’s most depraved, and it’s clearly very aware how Jack and even Amber are both complicit in that abuse- the “are we still friends” scene between Jack and The Colonel is my favorite example of this. Where it fails is in loving Jack too much, in genuinely buying his “last true artist” shtick even as it pokes countless holes in it, and so you’re left with a work that loves, sincerely, the prostitute and the whore- but also, naively and unfortunately, also loves the pimp and the wife-killer.

IM SORRY IM SORRY I just feel it’s a good movie but I don’t think it’s anything better than that or a masterpiece.I definitely don’t think this is a masterpiece. I enjoyed the movie but it wasn’t my favorite. Still a good ass movie tho. I was surprised how many actors were in this movie. Like seriously whoever was the casting director cooked. And also bro Paul Thomas Anderson was in his late 20s when he made this! That’s crazy. But yeah. I also find it funny how embarrassed Mark Wahlberg is of this movie even though this is probably his best performance from all of his movies. Same with Burt Reynolds. But I digress. Let’s go over what I liked about the film and what I wouldn’t say dislike but what I wasn’t big on in the film. 

Let’s start with the writing. It was good. Not great but good. Paul Thomas Anderson did a good job with his writing. The dialogue is pretty fun, I like that the writing doesn’t shy away from how awful the porn industry can be,and I really like how distinct each character is. Each character in this movie is pretty great and distinct. It's really great and hard to do. There’s a ton of characters in this movie and a lot of movies would forget a few characters and give them no characterization but this movie did a good job at giving everyone a distinct character which is cool and the main cast is pretty likable. I think my favorite story out of all the characters has to be Buck. He had a strong side story. I also like that we see how pornos had at least some effort put into it in the 70s while in the 80s pornos became easy to make and nobody cares about the quality of the pornos as long as it has sex in it. For the  directing, the directing is pretty amazing. I am not big on this movie but woah Paul Thomas Anderson knows how to direct. The aesthetics of this movie is amazing,the camera movement is amazing,the directing when it comes to acting is awesome. Like he made Julianne Moore act like a “bad actress” not only do I credit Julianne Moore for the performance but I have a feeling he definitely helped with that scene of Julianne Moore being a bad actor. I also think we have to give credit to Paul Thomas Anderson as a director because the dude brought out the best performance in Mark Wahlberg. Mark Wahlberg is always known for having a lot of bad performances like in the Transformers films,Scoob,and The Happening and even then he’s a mediocre actor. The only movie before this I really liked that he was, was the Departed but that’s because the movie takes place in Boston and he’s not doing anything crazy with his performance. But here I don’t see Mark Wahlberg being Mark Wahlberg, that's Dirk Diggler. Like damn he’s actually really great as Dirk I wasn’t expecting it. He does a great job as protagonist and makes you feel bad for Dirk when his life falls apart. He’s also really great at matching other actors. He doesn’t get out acted by Burt Reynolds,Julianne Moore,or John C Reilly. Other things I like about Paul Thomas Anderson directing is the staging like the way the party scenes are staged is great, Paul Thomas Anderon does a great job at making this feels like we’re in 70s and 80s California,he’s also really great with building up tension like the firecracker scene with Alfred Molina or the scene where William H Macy character decides to kill Nina Hartley or when everything goes to shit for all of the characters. He’s surprisingly great at building tension. So yeah. The cinematography is great like this is a pretty looking movie and I love how the colors are used throughout the movie. The acting is amazing. I already mentioned the Julianne Moore scene of her being a “bad actress” and Mark Wahlberg being great. But on top of that John C Rielly is great in this, I am so used to him being in comedic stuff that seeing him actually show his range is great even though he still has his comedic moments in this movie,Don Cheadle is great and funny as fuck in this, him looking like Rick James is hilarious, Burt Reynolds is great I should watch more stuff he’s in, Heather Graham is good as Roller Girl she’s great with raw emotions like the scene at the limousine, Phillip Seymour Hoffman is great as usual but I wish he was in this more, William H Macy is great, Luis Guzman is good and funny, and Nicole Ari Parker is good. And Alfred Molina was awesome in the one scene he’s in. To wrap this up the editing is great,the sound is good, the soundtrack is great and the song choices were great, the production design is great,and the casting is obviously great. I think my favorite scene in the movie is probably the firecracker scene just because Alfred Molina is acting his ass off. I also like the scene where Buck is trying to open a business. Like damn you feel bad for him. 

For the things I didn’t care about there’s a good amount. I found the second half very predictable. Like damn, as soon as the 80s section of the movie started after William H Macy's character decided to go out with a bang I knew how this movie was going to go. The reason why I say the second half was predictable is because this movie is literally just Goodfellas but for the porn industry. We built up how great this lifestyle is just to show the downside to the lifestyle and the characters going through a rough patch and a downfall. I knew immediately what I was going to get myself into. I also think this movie is way too long and I think the second half has a lot to do with it. Like there are side plots that take up a lot of time and I just found the second half less interesting compared to the first half. I just didn’t really connect with what the movie was trying to do in the second half and I felt like it dragged. Like yeah the firecracker scene is great because of the tension being built but at the same time we didn’t really need it. Like not really. The movie literally stoped and said “song Way Down(One Last Thing)” like what! It felt like an idea Paul Thomas Anderson came up with and was like this would be cool! Like even he knew this feels like a last addition. Idk. Maybe I am being harsh on this film but I wasn’t sold on what the second half was trying to sell me. It doesn’t make the movie bad but I didn’t care as much like I did earlier in the movie. One thing I didn’t care was the character of Todd the dude who got Dirk into that house with Alfred Molina character. He’s not supposed to be likable but he was just a nuisance of a character. And also unbelievably dumb. 

Overall this was a good movie. It’s not a masterpiece but I appreciate this movie for existing. It is surprising that this movie was made by a 26 year old. Like damn. I am almost 26 and I am not even close to making a movie yet. So that’s great. I hope Paul Thomas Anderson's other movies can impress me and live up to the hype.Like I want to see why One Battle After Another won Best Picture. I find it funny that this movie was being nostalgic about the 70s like how movies nowadays are nostalgic about the 80s and 90s. Just show that everyone is nostalgic about the previous decades no matter what generation it is. Watch people be nostalgic about the 2020s. I also find it crazy a movie about porngraphy was made in 1997. I bet there was a moral panic about a movie like this being made. There had to be. There are some great memorable scenes in this movie like William H Macy’s character finding Nina Hartley having sex with a guy on the pavement,Mark Wahlberg singing Touch, and Dirk arguing with Jack. And I actually like that the movie didn’t end on a downer. That was the one thing I didn’t predict about the second half. Bravo. So yeah. Good movie.

The needle drops and acting is a class part in this, but I really found it hard getting invested in the storyline or root for a particular protagonist. The film is really very underdeveloped in the first act, however the second act really brings it up from what I thought this movie was. Impressive work in many departments, I just could not see what the hype was about.

Oh to have lived through the 70s… There’s some great stuff, from King PSH’s usual standout superstar self, to the plethora of quotable one-liners, soundtrack (*although this was just peak era of music, so it’s lowkey cheating, and I actually think he relies on needle drops too much in this), to of course the dance sequence (a guaranteed Pers pleaser as a lover of the boogie). One thing I will credit PTA for, from every film of his that I’ve seen, is that he has mastered opening sequences. The first 3 minutes of his films are unanimously my favourite part. A mãe é agressiva e constantemente o humilha, enquanto o pai permanece passivo diante das discussões. O jovem finalmente encontra algo que nunca teve em casa: reconhecimento. As pessoas passam a admirá-lo, seu trabalho é elogiado e ele começa a ganhar prêmios.

Com o dinheiro, compra uma casa luxuosa, roupas caras e um Chevrolet Corvette laranja. Sua vida passa a ser organizada em torno da imagem de estrela que construiu para si mesmo.

### 5\. A mudança na indústria pornográfica

Enquanto os personagens enfrentam seus problemas pessoais, a indústria começa a passar por uma transformação.

Floyd Gondolli, um empresário interessado na distribuição de filmes pornográficos, procura Jack e propõe uma mudança na maneira como as produções são realizadas. Ele acredita que o futuro está no vídeo, que permite filmagens mais baratas e rápidas.

Desiludido com o rumo das produções, Jack tenta encontrar uma maneira diferente de trabalhar. Decide sair com Rollergirl e uma pequena equipe dentro de uma limusine, procurando homens desconhecidos nas ruas para filmar encontros sexuais espontâneos.

A experiência evidencia a vulnerabilidade de Rollergirl. Apesar de sua aparente segurança, ela continua carregando a vergonha de ser reconhecida por alguém de seu passado, e sua reação violenta é também uma tentativa de se defender dessa exposição.

### 7\. A derrota de Amber na disputa pela guarda do filho

Em 1983, Amber enfrenta um processo judicial para recuperar a guarda de seu filho. Seu ex-marido utiliza sua participação na indústria pornográfica, seu histórico criminal e seu vício em cocaína como argumentos para demonstrar que ela não seria uma mãe adequada.

Amber comparece ao tribunal esperando conseguir uma oportunidade de voltar a conviver com o menino, mas o resultado é desfavorável. A Justiça considera que ela não reúne condições para exercer a maternidade e mantém a guarda com o ex-marido.

A derrota a abala profundamente. Fora do ambiente profissional, onde é respeitada e reconhecida, Amber continua sendo julgada por suas escolhas e não consegue recuperar o vínculo familiar que perdeu.

Sua trajetória é uma das mais dolorosas do filme: ela encontrou naquele grupo uma família substituta, mas isso não foi suficiente para preencher a ausência do próprio filho.

### 8\. Buck tenta construir uma vida fora da pornografia

Buck conhece Jessie St. Vincent, outra atriz da indústria, durante a festa de Ano-Novo. Os dois se aproximam, começam um relacionamento e acabam se casando. Jessie engravida, e Buck passa a enxergar a possibilidade de construir uma família.

Ele continua interessado em abandonar a pornografia e abrir uma loja de equipamentos de som. Entretanto, quando procura financiamento bancário, descobre que seu passado profissional é um obstáculo. O banco não aceita conceder o empréstimo por causa de sua ligação com a indústria pornográfica.

A frustração aumenta porque Buck percebe que, apesar de trabalhar e tentar construir uma vida convencional, continua sendo definido por sua antiga ocupação.

Certa noite, enquanto está numa loja de rosquinhas, acontece um assalto. O criminoso entra armado e começa a ameaçar as pessoas. Um cliente também está armado, e a situação termina num tiroteio. O funcionário da loja, o assaltante e o cliente armado morrem.

Buck é o único sobrevivente. Em meio à confusão, consegue sair com o dinheiro do estabelecimento.

O episódio acaba lhe proporcionando uma oportunidade inesperada: ele finalmente consegue o capital necessário para abrir seu próprio negócio.

### 9\. A queda de Dirk Diggler

Enquanto isso, Dirk começa a perder o controle sobre a própria carreira.

O consumo de cocaína afeta sua capacidade de trabalhar e sua relação com as pessoas. A fama, que antes lhe proporcionava confiança, passa a alimentar sua arrogância. Ele acredita que é indispensável e começa a tratar mal aqueles que o ajudaram a chegar ao sucesso.

Sua relação com Jack se deteriora. O diretor tenta aconselhá-lo, mas Dirk já não aceita ser orientado. Também se afasta de Amber e passa a enxergar sua posição de estrela como algo que lhe garante privilégios permanentes.

Reed continua ao seu lado, mas os dois começam a desperdiçar o dinheiro com drogas e projetos que não dão resultado. Convencidos de que poderiam se tornar músicos, procuram produzir uma gravação demonstrativa para tentar ingressar no mercado musical.

A ideia é financiada com dinheiro que já não possuem. Quando chegam ao estúdio, descobrem que não conseguem pagar pelo trabalho.

A situação financeira se agrava. Dirk e Reed gastam o que resta, e a carreira do primeiro entra em colapso. Ele já não consegue manter o padrão de vida que construiu e começa a procurar outras maneiras de conseguir dinheiro.

Em determinado momento, Dirk passa a se prostituir. Durante um encontro, é agredido e roubado por três homens. A violência o deixa ainda mais desesperado, e ele percebe que perdeu o prestígio que antes parecia protegê-lo.

### 10\. A tentativa de golpe contra Rahad Jackson

Sem dinheiro e sem perspectivas, Dirk e Reed se aproximam de Todd Parker, um conhecido que também está envolvido com drogas e pequenos golpes.

Os três planejam enganar Rahad Jackson, um traficante rico e excêntrico que vive numa casa luxuosa. A ideia é vender a ele uma quantidade de bicarbonato de sódio, fingindo que se trata de cocaína.

Dirk e Reed acreditam que conseguirão receber o dinheiro e sair rapidamente, antes que Rahad ou seus homens percebam a fraude.

A casa de Rahad é um ambiente caótico. Ele passa boa parte do tempo consumindo drogas, ouvindo música em volume alto e disparando fogos de artifício dentro da propriedade. A situação é tensa desde a chegada dos três.

Durante a negociação, Dirk e Reed ficam cada vez mais desconfortáveis. Eles querem concluir a venda e ir embora, mas Todd, sob efeito de drogas e armado, decide tentar roubar dinheiro e outras substâncias da casa.

A situação explode quando Todd ameaça os homens de Rahad. Um tiroteio começa e ele consegue matar o guarda-costas do traficante, mas acaba sendo atingido por Rahad, que o mata.

Dirk e Reed conseguem escapar por pouco. A tentativa de golpe termina em desastre, e os dois percebem que chegaram a um ponto em que suas escolhas podem custar a própria vida.

### 11\. A reconciliação com Jack

Depois da fuga, Dirk finalmente reconhece que perdeu o controle de sua vida. Sem dinheiro, sem prestígio e sem a confiança das pessoas que o cercavam, retorna à casa de Jack.

Ele procura o diretor e admite, ainda que de maneira indireta, que precisa voltar a trabalhar. Jack o recebe, mas a relação entre os dois está profundamente marcada pelo que aconteceu.

Dirk também volta a se aproximar de Amber. Os três começam a reconstruir a relação profissional e afetiva que existia no início, embora nada possa retornar exatamente ao que era antes.

Reed, por sua vez, tenta encontrar seu próprio caminho e passa a trabalhar com apresentações de mágica em clubes noturnos.

A antiga equipe começa a se reorganizar, agora sem a ilusão de que o sucesso será permanente.

### 12\. O destino dos personagens em 1984

O filme avança até 1984 e apresenta o que aconteceu com os principais integrantes daquele grupo.

Buck finalmente consegue abrir sua loja de equipamentos de som. Sua esposa, Jessie, dá à luz o filho do casal, e Amber participa da produção de um comercial para divulgar o estabelecimento. Apesar dos obstáculos, Buck consegue realizar parte do sonho que alimentava desde o início.

Maurice Rodriguez também abre uma nova boate, desta vez com a ajuda de seus irmãos. Ele continua tentando construir seu espaço no ramo do entretenimento.

Rollergirl começa a frequentar aulas para obter o diploma equivalente ao ensino médio, numa tentativa de construir uma alternativa para sua vida.

Reed continua trabalhando com mágica e se apresenta em clubes. Embora não tenha alcançado o sucesso que imaginava, encontrou uma atividade que lhe permite continuar vivendo.

O Coronel permanece preso, e sua antiga posição de financiador já não tem importância para o grupo.

Jack, Amber e Dirk voltam a preparar uma nova produção. A indústria mudou, as pessoas envelheceram e o entusiasmo do passado foi substituído por uma realidade mais difícil, mas eles ainda tentam continuar trabalhando.

### 13\. A cena final: Dirk diante do espelho

Antes de começar a filmagem, Dirk está sozinho em seu camarim. Usa roupas que remetem à aparência de um astro televisivo dos anos 1980, especialmente ao estilo de Don Johnson em Miami Vice.

Ele observa o próprio reflexo e começa a repetir frases de incentivo. Diz a si mesmo que é uma estrela, que está preparado e que conseguirá realizar seu trabalho.

Depois, abre as calças e observa o próprio órgão sexual, como se estivesse tentando recuperar a confiança que possuía no auge da carreira. A câmera finalmente revela aquilo que durante boa parte do filme havia sido tratado como o grande atributo responsável por sua fama.

Dirk continua diante do espelho, ensaia alguns golpes de karatê e se prepara para sair.

O filme termina com ele retomando sua pose de estrela, pronto para voltar às filmagens.

### O significado do desfecho

A última cena é particularmente importante porque não representa exatamente uma vitória de Dirk. Ele conseguiu retornar ao trabalho, mas não recuperou a posição que possuía no final dos anos 1970. O que resta é a tentativa de reconstruir uma identidade que havia sido inteiramente sustentada pela fama.

O filme começa com um jovem que encontra naquele grupo o reconhecimento que sua família nunca lhe ofereceu. Jack, Amber e os demais tornam-se uma espécie de família substituta, e a indústria pornográfica aparece inicialmente como um espaço onde pessoas marginalizadas conseguem encontrar trabalho, amizade e algum sentimento de pertencimento.

Mas essa comunidade também está sujeita às mesmas contradições que qualquer outro ambiente: vaidade, exploração, dependência, competição e solidão. A liberdade que parecia existir naquele universo não impede que seus integrantes sejam destruídos pelas próprias inseguranças e ambições.

A transformação da película em vídeo acompanha essa mudança. Jack desejava fazer filmes com identidade cinematográfica, mas acaba submetido a um mercado que prioriza economia e produtividade. A decadência de Dirk e a perda de autonomia do diretor caminham paralelamente à transformação da indústria.

No fim, ninguém retorna verdadeiramente ao ponto de partida. Alguns conseguem construir uma vida diferente, outros continuam presos às próprias frustrações. Dirk, especialmente, precisa voltar a interpretar o personagem que criou para sobreviver: a estrela Dirk Diggler. O espelho mostra que, mesmo depois de perder quase tudo, ele ainda depende dessa imagem para acreditar em si mesmo.
